statement: In adults without heart disease when they joined prospective cohort studies, mostly in high-income countries, drinking a little compared with not drinking is associated with less coronary heart disease, but how much less depends on who is counted as not drinking, and no paper read gives absolute risks, so the ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. Against non-drinkers as each study defined them (in most studies people not drinking at the start, including former drinkers), people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 (95% CI 0.66 to 0.77) for new coronary heart disease (29 studies) and 0.75 (0.68 to 0.81) for coronary death (31 studies); at 2.5 to 14.9 g of ethanol a day (up to about one drink, counted as 12.5 g where a study gave no grams) the figures were 0.75 (0.65 to 0.88) and 0.79 (0.73 to 0.86), below 2.5 g a day 0.96 (0.86 to 1.06) and 0.92 (0.80 to 1.06), and at every higher intake, up to more than 60 g a day, 0.66 to 0.79; 8 of the 84 cohort reports gave only unadjusted estimates (Ronksley et al., 2011). In the 7 to 9 studies that compared with lifetime abstainers the figures were similar (0.73, 0.61 to 0.88; 0.75, 0.66 to 0.85), and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31, 1.02 to 1.68; against non-drinkers in the paper's table, against people who drank in its text). A review that compared only with lifetime abstainers and kept men, women, deaths and new cases apart (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; 24 studies) found lower point estimates at about one drink of 12 g a day in all four groups, but men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27); with all 44 studies, including those that combined men and women or deaths and new cases, every estimate at about one to three drinks a day was lower (0.62 to 0.81), and occasional drinking (less than weekly, or under 2.5 g a day) was not associated with coronary risk in any group. Of 23 conditions in the GBD 2016 curves fitted to 592 studies, only ischaemic heart disease showed a significant dip, lowest at 0.83 drinks of 10 g a day in men (relative risk 0.86, 95% uncertainty interval 0.80 to 0.96) and 0.92 in women (0.82, 0.72 to 0.95). Self-reported drinking showed the same dip in Chinese men (Millwood et al., 2019) and in UK Biobank, where allowing for smoking, body mass index, physical activity, cooked vegetable and red meat intake and self-rated health removed the statistically clear difference at moderate intake (more than 8.4 to 15.4 US drinks of 14 g a week) and, read approximately from the paper's figure, reduced but did not remove it at light intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). Whether alcohol causes the lower risk is disputed: in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand, former drinkers had more coronary deaths than lifetime abstainers (men 1.25, women 1.54), and in men drinking 60 g a day or more the lower risk seen against current non-drinkers (0.75, 0.63 to 0.89) was not seen against lifetime abstainers (1.00, 0.74 to 1.36; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014); genetic studies do not find the lower risk (see the answer on gene studies). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
plain: In many long-term studies, people who drank a little (up to about one drink a day) had about a quarter less heart disease than people who did not drink. But the people who did not drink included some who had stopped, perhaps because they were ill. When people were compared only with people who had never drunk, and men, women, deaths and new cases were kept apart, the difference in men's heart deaths was small and could be chance. In a large UK study, allowing for smoking, weight, exercise, diet and health made the difference at moderate drinking no longer clear. Studies using genes did not find it. So it is not known whether alcohol itself lowers heart risk, and none of these studies says how many people out of 100 the difference would mean.
population: Adults without cardiovascular disease at baseline in prospective cohort studies (and, in one review, case-control studies) published 1980 to 2010, mostly from high-income countries (84 cohort reports; 44 studies); the 592 studies behind the GBD 2016 curves; and the China Kadoorie Biobank (men) and UK Biobank cohorts
exposure: Drinking at baseline, self-reported, in grams of ethanol a day: Ronksley et al. under 2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60 and over 60 g/day (12.5 g per drink where a study gave no grams); Roerecke & Rehm occasional, 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99 and 24–35.99 g/day (about 1, 2 and 3 drinks of 12 g); GBD 2016 standard drinks of 10 g; UK Biobank US standard drinks of 14 g a week
comparator: Non-drinkers as each study defined them, in most cohorts current non-drinkers including former drinkers (Ronksley et al.); lifetime abstainers (Roerecke & Rehm 2012, and subsets in Ronksley et al.); each study's non-drinking category with a covariate for former drinkers (GBD 2016); abstainers at baseline (UK Biobank); non-drinkers and ex-drinkers plotted against the lowest-intake drinkers (China Kadoorie Biobank)
outcome: Coronary (ischaemic) heart disease: new cases (fatal or non-fatal heart attack, angina, ischaemic heart disease or revascularisation) and coronary deaths
magnitude: Ronksley et al. 2011 (prospective cohorts to September 2009; against non-drinkers as each study defined them, mostly current non-drinkers including former drinkers; each study's most-adjusted estimate, unadjusted for 8 of 84): any drinking, incident CHD RR 0.71 (0.66–0.77; 29 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.68–0.81; 31), CVD mortality 0.75 (0.70–0.80; 21); I² 72.2%. By intake (under 2.5, 2.5–14.9, 15–29.9, 30–60, over 60 g/day): incident CHD 0.96 (0.86–1.06), 0.75 (0.65–0.88), 0.66 (0.59–0.75), 0.67 (0.56–0.79), 0.76 (0.52–1.09); CHD mortality 0.92 (0.80–1.06), 0.79 (0.73–0.86), 0.79 (0.71–0.88), 0.77 (0.72–0.83), 0.75 (0.63–0.89). Against lifetime abstainers: incident CHD 0.73 (0.61–0.88; 9 studies), CHD mortality 0.75 (0.66–0.85; 7), CVD mortality 0.82 (0.78–0.86; 9). Former drinkers (against non-drinkers by the table, against drinkers by the text): CHD mortality 1.31 (1.02–1.68), CVD mortality 1.48 (1.23–1.79), incident CHD 1.10 (0.91–1.33). Roerecke & Rehm 2012 (44 studies to April 2010; against lifetime abstainers; former drinkers excluded and mortality corrected for them): fully stratified studies at 2.5–11.99, 12–23.99, 24–35.99 g/day, men's IHD mortality 0.89 (0.79–1.00), 0.86 (0.73–1.02), 0.78 (0.63–0.97); men's morbidity 0.77 (0.65–0.92), 0.75 (0.64–0.88), 0.74 (0.53–1.02); women's mortality 0.84 (0.74–0.96), 1.03 (0.84–1.27), 0.89 (0.57–1.40); women's morbidity 0.54 (0.45–0.65), 0.61 (0.38–0.99), 0.40 (0.14–1.13); occasional drinking 0.82 to 0.98, none significant; all 44 studies 0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1 (occasional 0.87 to 0.97, none significant); I² up to 84%. GBD 2016 (592 studies; against each study's non-drinking category, adjusted for former drinkers in it): IHD minimum RR 0.86 (95% UI 0.80–0.96) in men at 0.83 and 0.82 (0.72–0.95) in women at 0.92 standard drinks (10 g) a day; no significant dip for any other of 23 outcomes. UK Biobank (Biddinger et al. 2022): J- or U-shaped conventional associations; the moderate-intake difference for coronary artery disease not significant after six lifestyle factors (no values printed). China Kadoorie Biobank men (Millwood et al. 2019): conventional U shape for heart attack and CHD (no values printed for non-drinkers). Second-hand (Roerecke & Rehm 2014): former drinkers against lifetime abstainers, IHD mortality men 1.25 (1.15–1.36), women 1.54 (1.17–2.03); men drinking 60 g/day or more, IHD mortality 1.00 (0.74–1.36) against lifetime abstainers, against Ronksley et al.'s 0.75 (0.63–0.89) against current non-drinkers above 60 g/day. No absolute risks in any paper read.

evidence.extracted: An essay, with no methods, data or effect estimates of its own, arguing that Mendelian randomization is an instrumental-variable method subject to confounding, weak-instrument bias, pleiotropy, adaptation and failure of replication; that the example of alcohol and cardiovascular disease shows it must be treated with the caution due to all observational epidemiology; and that it should be renamed genetic instrumental variable analysis, without the words randomization or causality.

risk_of_bias.note: Both reviews are rated critically low on AMSTAR 2 (cards sc_ronksley_2011, sc_roerecke_2012) and neither appraised the risk of bias of the cohorts. In most cohorts the comparison group included former drinkers, some of whom stopped because of illness; 8 of 84 reports gave only unadjusted estimates and 11 of 44 studies adjusted for age only; in UK Biobank six lifestyle factors removed the association at moderate intake. These biases can change the estimate materially: against lifetime abstainers, with men, women, deaths and new cases kept apart, men's coronary deaths at about one or two drinks a day were no longer clearly lower.

inconsistency.note: The direction is consistent (by the authors' account, all but one to two study estimates per coronary outcome below 1). Statistical heterogeneity is high (I² 72.2%; up to 84%) and follows partly the reference group, sex and end point, which is the risk-of-bias problem and is not rated twice; women's coronary deaths at about two drinks a day (1.03) are an exception.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: an association in the cohorts studied, mostly in high-income countries, with drinking measured once at baseline.

imprecision.note: The pooled estimates are precise; the stratified lifetime-abstainer estimates are not, which the statement says.

publication_bias.note: Begg's test P 0.089 to 0.75 (Ronksley et al.); one of the Peters' tests positive (Roerecke & Rehm 2012); not rated down.

large_effect.note: Relative risks of 0.71 to 0.79; not large.

dose_response.note: No gradient: coronary risk is similar from 2.5 g to more than 60 g a day against current non-drinkers (an L shape), which does not fit a protective dose–response.

plausible_confounding.note: The remaining confounding (healthier habits of people who drink lightly; illness among former drinkers) would more plausibly exaggerate than hide the lower risk; no upgrade.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (comparison groups that include former drinkers, incomplete adjustment, and confounding shown directly in UK Biobank), so very low. Rated as worded: an association; whether alcohol causes it is the question of the debate box. Overlapping evidence is counted once: the two reviews share many cohorts, the GBD 2016 curves are fitted to largely the same studies and are model estimates used here only for the shape of the ischaemic heart disease curve, and the UK Biobank and China Kadoorie analyses are single cohorts. The many primary cohorts agree in direction, but the status is contested rather than replicated, because published critiques (Roerecke & Rehm 2012 and 2014 on the reference group; Biddinger et al. 2022 on lifestyle) and the genetic studies change how the association is read, and the reviews' own authors read it differently.

debate.question: Does drinking a little lower the risk of heart disease, or do the comparisons in cohort studies only make it look that way?
debate.evidence_yes: The lower risk is one of the most consistent findings of cohort studies. In 84 cohort reports published to 2009, people who drank had pooled relative risks of 0.71 for new coronary heart disease and 0.75 for coronary death against non-drinkers, with nearly every study's estimate below 1 by the authors' account, and the figures were similar in the 7 to 9 studies that used lifetime abstainers (0.73 and 0.75) (Ronksley et al., 2011; sc_ronksley_2011). With former drinkers removed and mortality estimates corrected for them, all 44 studies in a second review gave lower risks at about one to three drinks of 12 g a day in men and in women, for deaths and for new cases (0.62 to 0.81, every interval excluding 1) (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012; sc_roerecke_2012). The GBD 2016 curves, adjusted for former drinkers in the reference group for this condition, show a significant dip for ischaemic heart disease alone among 23 conditions (0.86 in men and 0.82 in women at just under one drink of 10 g a day; sc_griswold_2018), and self-reported drinking shows the dip again in Chinese men and in UK Biobank (sc_millwood_2019; sc_biddinger_2022). In seven studies, people averaging under 30 g a day without heavy drinking days had a relative risk of 0.64 against lifetime abstainers (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014; sc_roerecke_2014). Short-term experiments, cited second-hand, show alcohol raising HDL cholesterol and lowering platelet activation and fibrinogen, and the authors of two of the reviews argue on Hill's criteria that the association, at least for regular light drinking, is causal (Ronksley et al., 2011; Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). A published critique argues that the genetic studies pointing the other way have biases of their own (Mukamal et al., 2020; sc_mukamal_2020).
debate.evidence_no: Much of the lower risk depends on the comparison group and on adjustment. Most cohorts counted former drinkers among non-drinkers, and former drinkers had more coronary deaths (1.31 in Ronksley et al.'s table; against lifetime abstainers, men 1.25 and women 1.54 in the same team's earlier review, cited second-hand by Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). With lifetime abstainers as the comparison and men, women, deaths and new cases kept apart, men's coronary deaths were not clearly lower at about one or two drinks a day (0.89, 0.79 to 1.00; 0.86, 0.73 to 1.02) and women's were not lower at about two drinks (1.03, 0.84 to 1.27), and the authors concluded that a cardioprotective association cannot be assumed for all people who drink, even at low intake (Roerecke & Rehm, 2012). In UK Biobank, people who drank lightly or moderately smoked less, had lower body mass index, were more active and reported better health than people who did not drink, and allowing for six such factors removed the clear difference at moderate intake (Biddinger et al., 2022). The shape of the cohort results also fits bias better than benefit: against current non-drinkers coronary death was as low above 60 g a day as at one drink (0.75), with no gradient, while in men drinking 60 g or more it was not lower against lifetime abstainers (1.00, second-hand). Genetic studies, which are less exposed to these biases, do not find a lower risk: a variant that makes people drink less went with less, not more, coronary heart disease (0.90; Holmes et al., 2014; sc_holmes_2014), and in Chinese men the dip seen with self-reported drinking was absent when men were grouped by genotype (heart attack 0.96, 0.78 to 1.18, per 280 g a week; Millwood et al., 2019) (see the answer on gene studies). The experiments measure markers, not heart disease, and HDL cholesterol is also raised by heavy drinking and is highest in people with alcohol use disorder (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014).
debate.neither_can_show: No long-term randomized trial of drinking and heart disease exists (Roerecke & Rehm, 2014). The cohorts measured drinking once, by self-report, mostly in high-income countries, and cannot fully separate alcohol from the health, habits and social position of people who choose to drink a little; lifetime abstainers, too, may differ from people who drink in ways that were not measured. The genetic studies test lifelong differences in drinking and cannot show the shape of the curve at low intake with confidence (see the answer on gene studies). No paper read gives absolute risks, so how many heart attacks any difference would mean cannot be said. The reviews share many cohorts, and the GBD 2016 curve is fitted to largely the same studies, so their agreement is not independent replication.
debate.editors_reading: Editors' reading (certainty: very low). The sources agree that, in cohort studies, people who drink a little have less coronary heart disease than people who do not drink; they disagree on why. The strongest argument for a real protective effect is how consistent the association is across cohorts, sexes and end points, and that in the pooled data it survives removing former drinkers from the comparison group (0.62 to 0.81). The strongest arguments against are that it shrinks or becomes uncertain when men, women, deaths and new cases are kept apart, that it weakened with fuller allowance for lifestyle in a large recent cohort, that against current non-drinkers it is as large at heavy intake as at light intake, and that genetic studies, with different weaknesses, do not reproduce it. On the evidence read, a lower coronary risk with light drinking is observed but has not been shown to be caused by alcohol; if there is an effect, these studies cannot say how large it is, and none gives an absolute risk. The editors do not read this evidence as showing harm to the heart from light drinking either; that question rests on the genetic studies and their critique (see the answer on gene studies).
debate.what_would_settle_it: A long-term randomized trial of light drinking against not drinking with heart disease as the outcome. Short of that: individual-level reanalyses of cohorts with lifetime drinking histories that separate lifetime abstainers, former and occasional drinkers, measure drinking and drinking pattern repeatedly and take account of health before the start, reported with absolute risks; set beside genetic analyses in several ancestries that can estimate the curve at low intake without dividing people by how much they say they drink. None of the sources read reports these.
